topic: Safe withdrawal of prednisolone therapy in adults with non-endocrine disease
page_contents_html:
Safe withdrawal of prednisolone therapy in adults with non-endocrine disease

This guidance is relevant to primary care and outpatient settings.

Use for: adult, non-pregnant patients who have received prednisolone 5 mg daily or more for 4 weeks or longer for a non-endocrine condition.

The suggested taper of higher doses is based on the European Society of Endocrinology and Endocrine Society joint clinical guideline on glucocorticoid-induced adrenal insufficiency.

accordion_sections.heading: Background
accordion_sections.html:
• Glucocorticoid-induced adrenal insufficiency can occur when people discontinue long-term prednisolone therapy.
  • Adrenal insufficiency may result in an adrenal crisis if it is not recognised. People may also experience fatigue and weight loss.
  • Slow tapering of prednisolone may help to reduce the likelihood of adrenal insufficiency when withdrawing prednisolone used for a non-endocrine disease.

accordion_sections.heading: Suggested prednisolone taper
accordion_sections.html:
The table reproduces the taper in the supplied D&G draft. Doses are expressed as the daily prednisone/prednisolone-equivalent dose used in the source guideline.

Current daily doseSuggested dose reductionTime interval
More than 40 mgDecrease by 5-10 mgEvery week
20-40 mgDecrease by 5 mgEvery week
10-20 mgDecrease by 2.5 mgEvery 1-4 weeks
5-10 mgDecrease by 1 mgEvery 1-4 weeks
5 mgIn the absence of clinical symptoms, or following negative testing for adrenal insufficiency, continue to decrease by 1 mg. If low-dose prednisolone preparations are not available, an alternative is to switch to hydrocortisone 20 mg and decrease by 5 mg.Every 4 weeks

accordion_sections.heading: Key messages
accordion_sections.html:
• Prednisolone therapy should be slowly withdrawn over several months to reduce the risk of adrenal insufficiency.
  • Higher doses of prednisolone can be reduced more rapidly, but once the patient is taking prednisolone 5 mg daily or less, the taper is slowed. There is the option to switch to hydrocortisone at this point to allow a more gradual reduction.
  • While undergoing a slow withdrawal of prednisolone at 5 mg daily or less, patients should be considered to have adrenal suppression. They require counselling about sick-day rules and steroid warning cards.
  • Most patients do not require assessment of adrenal function before or during a slow withdrawal of prednisolone and can start the slow taper immediately.

accordion_sections.heading: Who should have adrenal function assessed?
accordion_sections.html:
A small subset of patients require assessment of adrenal function before or during the slow withdrawal:

  • Patients assessed as being at low risk of adrenal insufficiency who may be able to stop prednisolone without a slow withdrawal.
  • Patients who develop symptoms of adrenal insufficiency during the slow taper of prednisolone.
  • Patients for whom information about the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis is required, for example before elective surgery.

accordion_sections.heading: Adrenal function testing and action
accordion_sections.html:
Adrenal function can be assessed by measuring an early-morning plasma cortisol or by performing a short Synacthen® test.

Patients should omit their morning dose of prednisolone before the test and take it immediately after the test has been performed.

Local validation required before publication: the cut-offs below are reproduced from the supplied D&G Word draft. D&G Endocrinology and Biochemistry should confirm them against the local cortisol assay and short Synacthen® test protocol.

ResultEarly-morning cortisolPost-Synacthen® cortisolAction
No recoveryBelow 100 nmol/LBelow 250 nmol/LDelay the taper and reassess in 2 months.
Partial recovery100-300 nmol/L250-430 nmol/LStart the slow taper.
Normal recoveryAbove 300 nmol/LAbove 430 nmol/LStop prednisolone completely.

notes_for_editor: V2 intentionally follows the supplied D&G Word draft closely in content and order.
The original sequence has been retained: background and scope, taper schedule, key messages, patients requiring adrenal assessment, then testing and interpretation.

Changes from the Word draft are limited to corrected spelling/grammar, clearer web formatting, clarification of prednisone/prednisolone-equivalent wording, and an explicit local-validation note for the cortisol and Synacthen thresholds.

Confirm the supplied early-morning cortisol and short Synacthen cut-offs with D&G Endocrinology and Biochemistry before publication. The 2024 joint guideline uses generic morning-cortisol guide bands of below 150, 150-300 and above 300 nmol/L and does not recommend routine dynamic testing.
Confirm that omitting only the morning prednisolone dose is sufficient for the local assay and testing protocol.
Confirm local sick-day-rule and steroid-warning-card wording and link the approved local patient information if required.
Add author, approver, version and review date after governance approval.
